Longer reads

Three stories, in full

Marcelline Osei

Neighbor → Regular member · Joined May 2024
"I moved two blocks from here alone, knowing nobody. I stayed that way for years — I got good at it, honestly."

Marcelline moved to the Portsmith District in the spring of 2020 — right into the lockdown. By the time the world opened up, she'd developed the efficient solitude of someone who had learned to need very little. She had her routes, her grocery store, her park bench. The neighborhood was a backdrop, not a community.

A flyer for the August 2024 potluck landed under her door. She almost didn't go. "It seemed like the kind of thing where everyone already knows each other and you're the weird solo person in the corner," she remembers. She went anyway, because she'd been making jollof rice all weekend and had too much of it.

She ended up talking to Declan Walsh for an hour and a half about urban soil chemistry. He gave her a cutting from his lemon verbena. By the following month, she was helping Rosa plan the September gathering. By November, she'd volunteered at two garden workdays and started a WhatsApp group with her immediate neighbors to coordinate watching the block during rainstorms.

"The jollof rice is what got me in the door," she says. "But the thing that kept me coming back was realizing there's nothing magic about Common Table. It's just people making it easy to say hello. I could have done that any time. I just didn't know how."

Theo & Baba Kurosaki

Father & son · Regular members since November 2023
"My father is 68 years old and I have never seen him cry. He cried that morning, a little, in the kitchen."

Theo Kurosaki moved back to the neighborhood three years ago after a decade in Seattle. He and his father Baba — who has lived on Caldera Street since 1982 — had grown close again in theory but not quite in practice. They had dinner every few weeks. They talked about soccer and the weather. They were polite in the way that people who love each other and don't know how to say so become polite.

Theo signed them both up for Rosa's bread-baking skill share mostly because he thought his father would like getting out of the house. Baba had different ideas. He arrived with a well-worn index card — his own mother's milk bread recipe, in her handwriting, which he'd been carrying in his wallet for forty years. He had never made it. He had never taught it to anyone. He was waiting, he said, for the right moment.

For three hours in the Common Kitchen, Theo and Baba stood at the same table and made bread together. Baba translated the recipe from Japanese as they went, explaining the techniques in a voice Theo had never heard from him before — quiet, careful, almost tender. The bread came out beautifully. They ate it at the table with Rosa and six strangers and it was, by general agreement, the best thing anyone had tasted all year.

Baba has attended every skill share since. He brought his dashi recipe in December and his gyoza technique in March. "I have been waiting a long time to share these," he told Rosa. "I just needed someone to open the door."

Simone Whitfield

Steward member · Joined February 2022
"When you're retired and widowed, the world gets very quiet in ways you didn't expect. Common Table turned up the volume."

Simone Whitfield taught high school English for thirty-one years. She retired in 2019, then lost her husband Marcus in 2021. She is, as she describes herself, someone who spent a lifetime in rooms full of young people arguing about books, and then found herself in a very quiet house.

Her daughter sent her a link to Priya's reading circle in early 2022. "I think she was worried about me," Simone says with a measured smile. The title that month was Giovanni's Room. She arrived with seven sticky notes and strong opinions. She has not run out of sticky notes or opinions in the four years since.

Simone is now a Steward member and participates in the monthly organizer calls, where she is reliably the most prepared person in the room. She suggested the neighborhood newsletter that Common Table now prints quarterly. She organized a reading circle specifically for teens after noticing there were none. She helped design the seed library filing system.

"People say old age is about slowing down," she says. "I don't believe that. I just needed to find the right rooms again." She pauses. "Also, Priya chooses better books than I did. I will never say this to her face."
